But it was all happening so fast, I don't really know how -- what you're supposed to say or how you're supposed to react at that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, would I be correct in saying that these exchanges would occur near the front lines and that the Muslims would be released into Muslim territory and the Serbs would be then released into their own territory? Is that how an exchange would work?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've never attended an exchange but yes, that would be it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to this day -- let me ask you, sorry, another question. There were actually exchange commissions set up during the war to conduct these exchanges; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, later on during the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever heard from anybody prior to this day that Milan Lukic was involved in the work of exchanging Serb and Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, and I'm not aware of any exchanges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking back on the days or on the events of this day, is it now your belief that Milan Lukic told these men that he would exchange them in order to keep them calm?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now when I look back -- I don't quite understand. If it were happening now? Are you asking me now if I have some knowledge about that? I'm not quite sure about the order, the sequence of things. I didn't quite understand what you meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you another question. None of these men were handcuffed or bound in any manner; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You now know that Milan Lukic lied to these men, that he did not take them to be exchanged, he took them to be killed. You now know that to be true; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your belief that he told them this lie to prevent these unbound, unhandcuffed men from fleeing or resisting what he was attempting to do to them?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that could be. That could be a possibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did his lie to these seven men make it easier for him to commit the crime against them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Isn't that a comment, or are you seeking an admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm seeking his opinion, having been there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not sure what his opinion is worth. If it constitutes an admission, it's worth something.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm essentially asking him to give us an opinion on the state of mind of the captives and how that was affected by statements made to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That wasn't your question, Mr. Groome. If you want to get an admission as to a fact, by all means you attempt to do so. He is the accused. But I'm not sure that his opinion on these sorts of matters are going to have any weight. He's not an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on Tuesday, you told us that Milan Lukic asked Susnjar for keys to a room, but Susnjar did not want to give him keys because Milan was very rude; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that Mr. Susnjar, an elderly janitor, stood up to Milan Lukic and these other men who were armed and refused his request for the keys?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Milan Lukic ever threaten Susnjar with a weapon or with his words to turn over the keys that he was looking for?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, he didn't. He did not threaten him with weapons or anything. Well, I did not hear it anyway, because I had gone out at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is the point in time when you went outside of the hotel with your colleague, Meho Dzafic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Milan Lukic or any of the others attempt to stop you when you went out of the lobby?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know. He had his back to me. Perhaps he did not see that. But he didn't do anything, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's outside of the hotel that Meho first says to you, "Mitar, could you please come with me if you can."

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We came out of the hotel and I know well we came out and stood by the pine tree, and Meho asked me for a cigarette so I offered him one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this stage, you still believed that Meho and the other six men were going to be taken to be exchanged; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Meho tell you why he wanted you to go to the exchange?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He -- no, not in so many words. He did not say that I should go to the exchange with him. But we worked together for a long time. I think that he was retired in 1990. But before that, we'd worked together for a long time, and on various occasions -- well, we were together in one company, and before that in the restaurant, in the Panos restaurant. That is where he spent most of his career, and that is where I also came to work, so I knew him well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The transcript is reading that your answer to this question is that "He did not say that I should go to the exchange with him." Are you now changing your answer as to whether Meho asked you to go to the exchange?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, not that I should come there, not to come along as a person who would do the exchange, that is what I meant, not as somebody who would be responsible for the exchange, just to come along.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if both you and Meho believed that he is going to be exchanged, meaning released into Muslim territory, why does he -- why is it necessary for you to go to the exchange?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought if anything would come out of it, well, how do you know, if anything would come out of it, if he had been captured, that they would have to go to the command first, to go through that. And I thought that there I could ask somebody to let him go, because he was of advanced age and he was ill, he had ulcer. And now this talk about this exchange, and you suddenly hear about that. You never knew about that, you never knew what that was and what the -- how those things were arranged or anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that Meho did not want to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, no. I would have asked them on his behalf. I just said, "What are they going to do to you?" and he said, "No, no, no, they are going and rounding up people in the villages and they are rounding up only our folk." But whatever he said, he cheated people, that's what he did. Had they known what would come to pass, whether they knew -- had they known about him, had they heard about him, they would have fled their homes, they wouldn't have been there. How shall I put it? He is -- he can deceive easily because he has a smooth tongue. He's very persuasive. I don't know how to put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, what I'm trying to get at is what are you to do at the exchange? Why is it that you are being asked to go to this exchange? If Meho is simply going to be released into Muslim territory, what is your function at that exchange?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meho says, "You're coming with me," and I would have come along, and I did. Now, I would have no role to play there, I wouldn't have it. I thought there would be a commission or something in Prelovo that came to Prelovo. You know, it happens in a split second so then I would intercede on Meho's behalf. Or whether those people were returned, whether they would be exchanged if -- you know, these are thoughts that go through your head. I don't know. They'd release people, maybe there was some conditions. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Meho ever ask you to go to the exchange in order that he might be allowed to return to Visegrad for a health condition? Did he ever say that to you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, he asked me to come with him, and I promised, I said, "Yes, I will, Meho." I'm telling you, he's an elderly man, and -- well, I don't know what it's all about, but we're going to see. I didn't know where. So I thought that it -- that that place should be in Prelovo, but that's what I think. And I -- now, how does he feel up there? That one is yelling, calling people out. All this, I don't know what to tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, drawing your attention to the interview on the 17th of November, I'm going to read a question and answer from that interview and ask you whether you admit or deny giving this answer. "Q. Well, if the exchange commission is there, why do they need Mitar Vasiljevic to go along with Meho to talk to them?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Meho asked me and I was going to request that he be let go to come back because he had a health condition. He had an ulcer, and I knew that he had been suffering of that for years, suffering from that for years." Do you admit that you gave that answer to that question on the 17th of November last year?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at some point you left the Vilina Vlas Hotel with this group --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I'm sorry to interrupt. Are you going to accept that that's the end of it? Are you going to ask whether it's true?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, was that true?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was your intent for going to the exchange, to ask that Meho could be returned to Visegrad to get medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to let him go. I knew that Meho was a very ill man. Not a very ill man, but he often had this -- he often had these bouts of pain because of his ulcer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Meho's son was with him as well, was he not?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Meho ask you to try to have his son released to come back to Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't. Let me put it this way: I cannot remember every minute detail of that conversation, but as we are talking, I'd given Meho a cigarette, he is smoking, Milan is coming from over there, "Get into the cars," angrily, and he approaches Meho and snatches the cigarette. He snatched his cigarette and threw it away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I'm very concerned as to what we're going to be asked to make of this later. The reason why the accused went with Milan Lukic and the other men is, I would have thought, one of the vital points in this case. Now, he gave an explanation in his statement back in November. When asked today why he went -- he was going to go to the exchange, you said, "Why is it that you are being asked to go to this exchange if Meho is simply going to be released into Muslim territory, what is your function at that stage?" And the accused said, "Meho says you're coming with me, and I would have come along, and I did. Now, I would have had no role to play there and I wouldn't have it. I thought there would be a commission or something." Now, there was no explanation then which is consistent with what he said in the statement. Now, I don't know which one you're going to accept in the end. I still don't understand it. But it seems to me that this is vitally important in this case as to why the accused went to the Drina River with these men, and I -- it may be that you're being too clever for me, but I have no way of understanding what the Prosecution case is on this from your cross-examination. And it is your obligation in cross-examination to put your case to the witness. Now, at some stage, before you keep going off to some other subject, I would like to know what the Prosecution case is about his motive for going. If you are going to lead up to it, I will let you do it, but you seem to be going off on another course all the time and not finishing on this particular matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution is simply seeking to impeach the witness with another inconsistent statement for the same conduct, that at various times the accused has given different reasons for his conduct. Simply that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Simply that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Nothing more clever than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's clever enough, I suppose, but I still, if I may say so, have been left in the dark and it's been making me very worried. But if that's your case, then you've probably put it sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at some point, Mr. Vasiljevic, you get into the vehicles and you leave with Milan Lukic and these other men; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at this point, you're still under the belief that no harm will come to these men, and that they are simply being taken to an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When is the first time that you realise that they are not being taken for an exchange?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whilst in Sase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened in Sase that led you to believe that you were not going to an exchange?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, he stopped in Sase and he made those people get out of the car. He ordered them to walk down to the river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any time before leaving the hotel, did you tell Milan Lukic that Stanko Pecikoza was looking for him?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "He will find me," something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What precisely did you say to Milan Lukic regarding Stanko Pecikoza?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That Stanko was looking for him, something to that effect. But he was very angry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he say to you when you told him this?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We'll find him," "I'll find him," something like that. He didn't talk much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the point you realise you are not going to an exchange, do you realise what Milan Lukic's intentions are?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were still in the car or after those people, the victims, got out of the car? When we got out of the car, is that what you mean? Are you referring to that moment, as we were going down to the river?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm asking you, at the moment that you realise you are not going to an exchange, do you know at that point in time what Milan Lukic really intends for these people?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as soon as he ordered them to walk to the river, I realised what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He ordered them to go down to the Drina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that point in time, was it clear to you that he intended to kill them?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I begged him, I said, "Milan, please don't. These people haven't done any harm to you. Leave them alone." But it was to no avail. He couldn't be persuaded. He was so angry. And I was trying to reason with him, to explain to him that I had known Meho for years. And I said, "Milan, please, for God's sake." It was such a terrible moment. And at one point in time he did hug Meho, he put his arm around him, but that was just his game.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you begged for the lives of all the men, not simply your friend Meho; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He could have brought other people, it could have been some other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is when you were begging Milan Lukic, you were asking him to spare all seven of their lives, not simply Meho's?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, all of them. I said, "These people haven't done anything wrong. What's happening with you? Are you normal?" And I was telling him that this person was my colleague, with whom I had worked for so many years. I was also afraid. I was afraid of god's wrath. But it was all to no avail. He simply couldn't be talked to. He kept going down to the river, and it was no use begging him. He didn't even let us talk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were begging Milan Lukic, would you characterise for us your tone of voice? Was it simply conversational or were you speaking loudly to him?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The usual tone. I was with him, I was with Meho, we were walking behind the rest of them. At one point in time, he put his arm around Meho, and I thought that he would have pity on him. But it happened all very fast. Those were just seconds, not even minutes. And the whole situation was so embarrassing, awkward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've testified that after the murders, you were terribly upset; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were quite upset not only because you witnessed this but because you lost a close friend and colleague; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I never saw it, I had never seen such a thing before. I don't know how to describe it. Terrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in the days after you witnessed this horrible killing, you never went and told the wife of Meho about her son's -- her husband and her son's death, did you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nor did I dare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the days after this murder, you never returned to the site of the murder and buried the body of your dear friend and colleague, did you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nor would it have been possible for me to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why would it have been impossible for you to do that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply couldn't. I don't think I would have been able to bear this. I was never in a position to -- I mean, I had already seen dead bodies, but I don't think I would have been able to recover his body, to take it. And it's not only Meho. I don't think I would have been able to do that with any other body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did tell us that you reported the crime to Dragan Tomic, the commander of the police; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you reported it the very next day; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told him all the names of the people who were involved; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he wrote down details of what you described for him.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also told us before that it was having witnessed this murder of these men that you realised just how dangerous these men were; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only later on, yes, what this exchange meant for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, knowing how dangerous these men are, you've asked us to refer to them by code numbers rather than using their name because of what they may do; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. VG3 and VG4 are not as dangerous as Milan, I mean far from that. He was the one who led everything. If he wanted to release those people and not to kill them, I don't think that VG3 and VG would be able to do anything about it. It's just the kind of man he is. He was the organiser. They simply accompanied him. Okay, they also did arrest Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. people, but he was behind everything. He was the mastermind. They wouldn't have been there if he hadn't suggested that. He is most probably the organiser of the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm asking you, Mr. Vasiljevic, is having learnt how dangerous these men were, having fears for your family, how was it that you went to the police, the very police that they were working with, to report their names as having committed this crime? Did you not have fears that they would cause harm to you and your family back then?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I asked the commander not to say that I was the one who reported it. Only maybe if he had managed to arrest them, I don't think in that case I would have been afraid. It's very -- it would have been very difficult for me had they known that I was the one who had reported that, and if they were still at large.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, would you agree with me that at the place where these murders took place, there are no houses, they are simply vacant fields on both sides of the river; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a meadow below the road, and yes, you are right, there are no houses on that meadow. But as you leave Sase, going towards Prelovo, there is an area which has some houses. However, at the very spot where this all took place, maybe 200 or 300 metres away from the spot, there are no houses at all. At the very spot where it all happened, there are no houses. But then once again, as you move along the road, up above the road there are two or three houses, and another one which was still under construction did not have a roof. It was not a finished house. Nobody lived there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, would you agree with me that, according to your version of these events, you were the only witness to that crime, the only person who witnessed the crime and did not participate in it? Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, sir, if I may, please. My children are coming to see me tomorrow, and if I did not have a weapon -- let my children suffer what all those victims suffered if I'm not telling the truth now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, would it not have been perfectly clear to Milan Lukic and these other two men who it was that reported this crime to Dragan Tomic? Wouldn't they have known that it had to have been you, it could only have been you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I asked him, I didn't want him to tell them that I was the one who reported that. Of course, if he had arrested them, I would have then been able to speak about it. But no one took any steps in that respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, your attorney has told us that there will be some witnesses testifying about your mental state at the time of these crimes. I would ask you now to describe for us what did you believe your mental condition was during June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did drink, I'm not trying to hide that fact. I was not well psychologically. My mental state was not okay. I was afraid, I experienced fear. I was under the influence of alcohol. I just wasn't myself. If I had been sober, I probably would have reacted better, I would have managed to perhaps exert some influence on Milan. I am sure that my conduct was not the same as it would have been if I had not been drunk. It's true, I drank, but I think that I was also unlucky in a sense. And then there was in cousin of mine who got killed, and I was not the only one in such a situation. There were lots of other men, soldiers, who were not simply well at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, you were able to appreciate that the crime that occurred on the 7th of June was wrong, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whatever problems you remember having with your alcoholism, it did not impede your ability to know that that was wrong, what happened; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course. After all, they were people. No, of course it was wrong, even if you're totally drunk. Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just regarding how much alcohol or when you last had alcohol, at the time of the killings, when was the last time that you had a drink that day?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean before the event? Maybe an hour and a half or two. I will be sincere with you. Even when I was at work, working at the bar, I would have a sip here and there. But when I was completely off alcohol, I wouldn't drink at all. But otherwise I drank almost constantly, and that's how I am when I drink.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasiljevic. Your Honour, I'm about to embark on a new area, and there are a couple of administrative matters. They should only take about five minutes. But would the Court wish me to continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no, if we can fill in some of the time. Mr. Vasiljevic, you can go back to sit -- you can return to your seat behind counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first matter is I have a repaginated, complete set of the accused's statement in his own language to replace the one that has seemingly become confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And are the pages numbered for him this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, they are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I also have the redacted copies of the statement for the Chamber and for Mr. Domazet, and they are already in evidence as P15. These would be the redacted copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I'd rather like to keep 15 as it stands, but we'll call it 15.1 if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you got any problems? You've checked these, have you, Mr. Domazet, these redactions? These are the redactions to protect witnesses' names.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. They will be Exhibit P15.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure if 15 is under seal. If it's not, I would ask that that be placed under seal, and 15.1 be the public ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well, then. Exhibit 15 will now be placed under seal. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That hardly took five minutes. Still. We'll write 15.1 on that. Very well. Then we'll adjourn now until 9.30 on Monday, the 12th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: One day we'll get out of the courtroom before you catch us, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to ask the Court's indulgence to allow me to talk to Mr. Vasiljevic for about five minutes, because we are not going to see each other for two weeks, and there was something I wanted to raise with him. I don't know if this is possible because he hasn't finished his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't want to know what it is that you want to raise with him, but is it safe to describe it as something to do with the future conduct of the proceedings rather than the evidence which he's given?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, just that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Groome, I've already pointed out to Mr. Domazet that there may be some comment passed or some inference drawn if the defendant changes his evidence on some point at this time, but it is a difficult situation we find ourselves in. I must say I never thought we would still be having the accused in the box at this stage. What's your attitude towards this?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Vasiljevic's ability to participate in the preparation of his defence is an extremely important right. I have known Mr. Domazet to be a man of honesty and integrity. If he assures us that he will not speak about his testimony, I would have no objection to him speaking to Mr. Vasiljevic about preparing his upcoming defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Does that satisfy you, Mr. Domazet, apart from the compliment?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, then. Thank you, Mr. Groome. That's a very sensible attitude to take. Now, can we go? All right, we'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 12th day of November, 2001, at 9.30 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
